title: computers.json
description: People have long archived technology, but there’s no in-between place where you can see the fine details of physical objects online. Computers.json is a public archive of people’s personal computers that doubles as a communal space on the web.

process_steps.text: I initially 3D scanned the computers with Polycam using photogrammetry.
Afterwards, I went into MeshLab to clean up the model, fill in the gaps, and optimize it, so that it would retain detail and display well on the web.
My next step was flatbed scanning the surfaces of the computer to capture high-resolution detail.
Then I took my scans into Blender and applied the flatbed scan textures to the 3D mesh. This created a high-resolution render of a 3D model without expensive equipment.

To further optimize the render on the webpage, I created a lower-resolution model that displays when the user first opens the page, which makes it load faster. Users can then choose to view the model in high resolution. Throughout my process, I wanted to keep as much detail in the 3D model as possible without sacrificing my users' experience on the webpage.

reflection.reflection_text: This project taught me a lot about optimizing 3D models and sparked my interest in computer graphics. People loved it, especially the community aspect. Although it started as a quick class project, I want to keep developing the website. I’ve made an open-source tutorial of my process so others can scan and submit their own computers, and I’m working to grow the archive. A good archive should be as full as possible, and I especially want to collect more weird, funky computers. That feels especially timely now that cyberdecks are back and computers are being hidden inside everyday products. I’m interested in how computing keeps changing in this new technological world, and in how a computer can be a far more personal, intimate object than the standard flat rectangle. This project was my attempt to bridge that gap by showing how people personalize their computers and the relationships they have with them.

description.description_text: A fashion search engine, digital closet, and community home all in one. Rooted in curation rather than overconsumption, it’s for those who love fashion beyond aesthetics. Inspired by 2000s outfit-generator games, Myspace, and early Pinterest, it brings the play of the old internet into a modern context, with node-based boards and an open sandbox for experimenting with your closet.

process_steps.text: Research: I begin by researching old website design and 2000s outfit-generator games to find which UI/UX elements made the web feel playful.
Sketch: I work quickly by sketching wireframes, focusing on how the system will look and how its parts will interact.

Iterate: I keep refining these sketches, testing ideas, cutting what doesn’t work, and redrawing until the interactions feel right. Because the sketches are quick, I can go through many versions without getting attached to any one.
Build: With my technical background, I can turn these sketches into working designs with ease. Building often shows new ideas, so I loop back to sketching as needed.

reflection.reflection_text: Although this was a prototype, watching people test these interactions during our final showcase sparked a lot of joy! There were still issues with web scraping to pull images from websites, which was tedious, so it isn’t yet viable as a large-scale application. Still, the core concepts came across to my audience. People enjoyed how experimental the interface was and felt it clearly communicated the app’s message. Overall, I want to keep iterating on this project and hopefully scale it to a larger context.

title: please, verify your identity
description: please, verify your identity is an interactive installation that performs consent theater. its “no” button flees your cursor until only “yes” remains, and the face you surrender is shredded byte by byte into colored noise that facial recognition can’t read. the piece mimics the rituals of digital trust (accept, scan, encrypt) to show how interfaces manufacture compliance, and asks what happens when the machine becomes the being and we become the interface.

title: real american
description: A life-size invisible green card, symbolizing legal residency while still labeling its holder a “Resident Alien.” This term dehumanizes immigrants and reinforces the idea that they will never be seen as “true Americans.” Anyone can walk into the frame to reflect on, empathize with, and humanize immigrants in the US.

title: reminiscence
description: A reinterpretation of sentimental childhood items that were lost, based on three individual interviews. These recollections tell a story of objects used to communicate the intangible: memories and feelings.

title: dreamscape
description: A love letter to growing up as a neurodivergent girl, told through the language of lolita fashion—a J-fashion subculture defined by anti-consumerism, feminism, and radical self-expression.
